name: Water test kits (pool, spa and drinking water, free chlorine)
summary: Tablets, drops or paper strips that show by colour how much chlorine is in water, made for pools and spas; one that reads free chlorine as low as 0.5 mg/L can check bleach-treated drinking water.
uses: Aim for at least 0.5 mg/L free chlorine after 30 minutes at pH below 8, longer if cold (WEDC Mobile Note 7, quoting WHO; MSF cholera; WHO chlorine test). WHO's 0.2 to 0.5 is for a supply's collection points; 0.2 is US EPA's pipe-network minimum (WHO chlorine test; Health Canada chlorine TD)
It can't detect germs: chlorine-resistant Cryptosporidium and Giardia are expected to stay unaffected, and bacteria in silt may not be reached (WHO chlorine test; Health Canada chlorine TD)
It measures only chlorine, so it says nothing about lead, nitrate, fuel or other chemicals; boiling and disinfection don't remove heavy metals, salts and most chemicals (WHO chlorine test; EPA water)
OTO (yellow) kits read total chlorine, not the free chlorine that kills germs; use a DPD (pink) kit (Taylor FAQ; San Bernardino pool kit)
Above about 10 ppm, chlorine can bleach DPD to a false low or zero: dilute and retest before adding more bleach (Taylor FAQ)
Restaurant chlorine sanitizer strips such as Hydrion's read 10 to 200 ppm, so they can't show 0.5 mg/L; a blank strip tells you nothing about it (Hydrion sanitizer strips)
identify: Pool and spa kits come as a clear plastic comparator with tablets or dropper bottles, or as a tub of paper strips with the colour chart on the label. DPD turns the water pink to red, and the deeper the colour, the more chlorine (WHO chlorine test; Taylor FAQ). OTO or OT kits turn it yellow and measure total chlorine only (Taylor FAQ). Free chlorine is what is left over to kill germs; combined chlorine has reacted with nitrogen and is no longer available to disinfect; total is the two added together (WHO chlorine test). Kits read in ppm or mg/L, which are the same for water (EPA data FAQ). The WHO's DPD comparator scale runs from 0.2 to 8 mg/L in its figure (WHO chlorine test), but San Bernardino County's minimum range for public-pool free-chlorine kits is 0.5 to 3 ppm (San Bernardino pool kit), so check that the lowest mark on your kit's chart is 0.5 mg/L or lower before you rely on it. On LaMotte's free-chlorine strips a white pad means a trace, such as 0.5 ppm, and the purple on the chart is clearly visible only at 1.0 ppm (LaMotte strip tips). Most pool kits also read pH and alkalinity, and some read cyanuric acid, the pool stabiliser (Taylor FAQ; San Bernardino pool kit). Kitchen sanitizer strips such as Hydrion's are made for sanitizing solutions and read 10 to 200 ppm, so they can't show 0.5 mg/L (Hydrion sanitizer strips). Home drinking-water strip kits may claim to test for lead, nitrate or bacteria. Health Canada says only tests done through an accredited lab or a public health unit are accurate and reliable (Health Canada well test).
test: 1. Date: read the expiry or best-by date on every bottle, tablet pack and strip tub (Taylor FAQ). Hydrion lists 2 years for its other products and 3 years from manufacture for its pH paper (Hydrion help). Taylor says to use the printed date, store reagents and strips at 2 to 29 °C, out of direct sun, away from treatment chemicals and tightly capped, and replace them seasonally (Taylor FAQ). Treat a kit that has baked in a car or shed, or a strip tub left open in damp, with suspicion. 2. Blank: test the untreated water first. 3. Known positive (our inference, no source tests it): dose a litre of clear water with 2 drops of plain unscented household bleach, the standard disinfecting dose (EPA water; Health Canada emergency water), stir, wait 30 minutes and test. That is many times the 0.5 mg/L target, so a working kit should show a strong colour, not a faint pink. If it reads zero or pale, it may be bleaching (step 4); if it is still zero after diluting, the reagent or the bleach is dead: try the other bottle of each. 4. A zero or faint reading on water you dosed heavily may be bleaching, not a lack of chlorine. Dilute it 1 to 1 with chlorine-free water, retest, and double the result (Taylor FAQ). 5. Strips are only accurate to about half the gap between two colour blocks (Taylor FAQ), so a colour between two blocks is only roughly that value. A DPD comparator like the one the WHO shows reads in steps from 0.2 mg/L (WHO chlorine test).

decay.note: Estimate. Hydrion lists 2 years for most products, 3 for pH paper (Hydrion help); Taylor says use the printed date, replace reagents each season and keep them out of sun and below 29 °C (Taylor FAQ). Fresh reagent can revive an old kit.

improvise: Without a kit, follow the dose and the wait exactly and don't skip either. Boil hard for at least 1 minute (at least 2 minutes above 2,000 m) (Health Canada BWA), or add 2 drops of plain unscented household bleach per litre, double it if the water is cloudy, coloured or very cold, stir and wait 30 minutes, or 1 to 2 hours below 10 °C (50 °F) (HealthLinkBC 49b). EPA's chart is for 6% or 8.25% bleach; Health Canada gives 2 drops, about 0.2 mL, of 5.25% bleach (Health Canada emergency water), so check the label. It should smell slightly of chlorine; if not, dose again and wait 15 minutes more (EPA water). People's taste and smell thresholds vary a lot, so smell is a rough check only (Health Canada chlorine TD). Let silty water settle and filter it first, because chlorine can't reach germs inside silt (WHO chlorine test). Bleach weakens with age: Clorox says it keeps up to a year away from heat and sun, then may be too weak to disinfect; Clorox bottles show the year and day of making in a code on the neck (Clorox date). Useless for safety: clear looks, taste and smell, since many contaminants don't change smell, taste or colour (Health Canada well test), and pH strips alone, because pH has no direct health effect, though it does change how well chlorine works (Health Canada pH TD). Water you suspect holds fuel, metals or other chemicals can't be fixed by chlorine or boiling: find another source (EPA water; WHO chlorine test).
